summary: High-level security review focused on encryption at rest/in transit and KMS/BYOK/HSM options. Titan cares about key custody and auditability; they are evaluating Redwood Private with BYOK for PCI-scope workloads. Discussed AWS/Azure/GCP KMS support, HSM integrations (PKCS#11), rotation, performance implications, and audit logging. Agreed to share docs and schedule a scoping session.

KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS)

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~51 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (Redwood SA); Daniel Cho (Titan CISO); Maya Rivera (Titan Head of Platform); Liam O'Connor (Titan Security Engineer); Sara Nguyen (Titan DevOps)

Summary (auto): Security review covering encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK, HSM options and operational considerations.

[00:00] Alex Morgan: hey everyone thanks for joining on time uh looks like we've got about 50 minutes on the calendar, we'll focus on encryption and key management, and leave time for any PCI/HSM specifics you want to dig into, sound good?
[00:12] Daniel Cho: yeah sounds good alex, we mostly want to understand who holds keys, what evidence we get, and any perf impacts to inference especially for low-latency payments flows.
[00:25] Priya Shah: cool, i'll start with a quick overview  redwood supports encryption in transit via TLS and encryption at rest for models and cache layers; for keys we integrate with cloud KMS providers and also support BYOK via EKM/HSM integrations.
[00:40] Maya Rivera: when you say "support" for BYOK, do you mean we can supply our own keys and you never see them? that's the requirement for our PCI scoped vector.
[00:55] Priya Shah: yes, in private deployments the control plane can be configured so that key material is only accessible to your KMS/HSM. Redwood can be configured to use customer KMS via standard APIs (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google KMS) or via PKCS#11 to talk to on-prem HSMs - in those cases we only get wrapped keys and never hold plaintext.
[01:20] Liam O'Connor: clarify "wrapped keys" — does that mean the service sends encrypted data to your runtime and you unwrap locally? what's the trust boundary.
[01:33] Jordan Lee: good question — implementation varies by deployment mode. In Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem), the inference nodes can be provisioned in your VPC and the key material remains in your KMS/HSM. We call the KMS to unwrap a data encryption key (DEK) that is cached in the node's secure memory (KV cache) for a configurable TTL. Redwood does not persist plaintext keys to disk.
[01:58] Daniel Cho: okay how about Dedicated/reserved hosted instances? we may still want BYOK for some dev/staging datasets.
[02:10] Priya Shah: for Dedicated we support customer KMS in a couple modes — bring-your-own-key via cloud KMS where Redwood's service is granted a decrypt/unwrap role with strict IAM, or a proxy where you shuttle wrapped keys. For hosted multi-tenant we can't do customer HSM attached, but we do offer envelope encryption and rotations, and we can provide audit logs and attestations.
[02:36] Sara Nguyen: are there any latency hits when the node calls KMS to unwrap? payments need <100ms in the critical path.
[02:48] Priya Shah: the common pattern is to unwrap a DEK and cache it; KMS calls happen on key rotation or cache miss. So per-inference KMS calls are not typical — they would be catastrophic for latency. The only time you'd see an extra RTT is first unwrap or after a node restart. That said if you want double wrap with client-side encryption that's possible but adds complexity.
[03:15] Daniel Cho: ok so runtime caching is key. what's the cache TTL and how is it protected?
[03:25] Jordan Lee: TTL is configurable — we've seen customers set 1-24 hours depending on their risk tolerance. Keys are held in secure process memory and the runtime can be configured to wipe on swap / OOM; for Private we recommend ephemeral instances with encrypted swap disabled. We can also integrate with HSMs that provide key usages so you can offload crypto ops if you don't want to store DEKs at all.
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: offload crypto ops meaning the HSM performs encryption/decryption per op? won't that add a huge latency?
[04:01] Priya Shah: yes if you require HSM to perform per-token crypto ops it would be high latency and probably impractical. Typically HSMs are used for key wrapping/unwrapping, signing, and rotation; heavy per-token ops remain in-node with DEKs.
[04:18] Maya Rivera: what's the HSM support matrix? vendors and protocols?
[04:24] Alex Morgan: we validate against common vendor stacks — AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, Thales/Cavium via PKCS#11, and on-prem partners. For private installs we can do PKCS#11 or gKMS proxy approaches. We'll share a compatibility matrix after the call.
[04:43] Daniel Cho: auditability — we need to show who invoked unwraps, rotations, and key creation. do you capture KMS audit logs or do we rely on our KMS?
[04:54] Priya Shah: audit logs originate from the KMS for key lifecycle events. Redwood emits correlated operational logs (node ID, request IDs, timestamps) to your audit pipeline — you can push them to your SIEM or we can forward a copy. For hosted we provide redwood-managed audit logs but for BYOK you should also keep KMS logs as ground truth.
[05:15] Sara Nguyen: and retention? our compliance wants 7 years for certain artifacts.
[05:22] Alex Morgan: we can provide log exports for retention; retention policies depend on the plan and add-on. We'll send exact export formats and retention SLAs.
[05:33] Daniel Cho: rotation policy — can we force rotate and revoke the DEKs quickly if needed? what's the failover?
[05:42] Jordan Lee: yes rotation is supported. When a KMS rotates a CMK you unwrap a new DEK and rewrap existing DEKs; Redwood supports lazy rewrap on access or background rewrap jobs. Revocation semantics depend on KMS — you can disable a key which prevents new unwraps; nodes with cached DEKs would need to be rolled or have TTL expire; we can coordinate a forced node restart/eviction via orchestration to flush caches.
[06:10] Liam O'Connor: that is an operational concern — we need a handshake mechanism so we can revoke and be sure no node is still using a key.
[06:19] Priya Shah: agreed, we can add an orchestration hook: key disable triggers a policy that marks nodes for immediate eviction; we also support short cache TTL for high-security apps. We'll document the recommended playbook.
[06:34] Daniel Cho: what about encryption in transit for internal RPCs between nodes and model shards?
[06:41] Jordan Lee: all node-to-node traffic in our runtime uses mTLS with mutual auth; certificates can be provisioned via your PKI or Redwood's internal CA depending on deployment. For Private we recommend using your PKI for full control.
[06:58] Maya Rivera: do you support hardware-attested enclaves or TEE for key protection?
[07:05] Priya Shah: we currently have integrations exploring Intel SGX and Nitro Enclaves for certain customers, but it's not broadly available as GA — we can discuss roadmap if that's a blocker.
[07:18] Daniel Cho: ok can you speak to data residency? some keys and metadata must stay in eu-west-1.
[07:25] Alex Morgan: region can be pinned. For RTC data and key operations you can restrict KMS to a specific region; for Private deployments you control the region entirely. Hosted customers can request regional tenancy for keys and artifacts.
[07:38] Liam O'Connor: will token-level telemetry ever include PII? we need assurance PII never leaves our control.
[07:46] Priya Shah: telemetry is configurable — we can exclude or redact token-level payloads. For PCI-scoped work we recommend Private with strict telemetry rules and redactions.
[08:00] Sara Nguyen: a question on key destruction: if we decommission keys how do you prove zero retention?
[08:07] Jordan Lee: KMS providers have defined destruction flows; Redwood will delete wrapped keys and remove any cached DEKs in memory; we can provide attestations and node-level evidence for key deletion. Again, for BYOK the KMS's destruction is the source of truth.
[08:25] Alex Morgan: quick pause — any questions so far on the high-level pattern?
[08:31] Daniel Cho: not yet, but i want to dig into perf with a real example — if we have a model that serves 200 RPS for fraud-scoring and each request hits KV cache and does a small model compute, where does KMS call affect SLO?
[08:46] Priya Shah: only at unwrap; so common flow: at node startup unwrap DEK (single call), cache DEK in memory; process requests using DEK locally. So for 200 RPS normal ops shouldn't touch KMS. If you had frequent node churn you'd see more KMS calls. Also cache warmup is important for peak window.
[09:07] Maya Rivera: how do you handle multi-tenant key separation when different teams or customers share a node?
[09:16] Jordan Lee: we recommend tenant isolation at node level for cryptographic separation; in Dedicated you can allocate tenant-specific pools. For hosted multi-tenant we use envelope encryption and strict namespace separation.
[09:30] Liam O'Connor: about HSMs — can Redwood integrate with our Thales network HSM over the network?
[09:37] Priya Shah: yes PKCS#11 over a network gateway is supported. We'll need a network path and firewall rules for the HSM gateway; we can run an HSM proxy in your VPC to minimize latency.
[09:50] Daniel Cho: firewall rules and network path — can you share a sample runbook?
[09:55] Alex Morgan: yes we'll add a runbook and a sample security group and route table config.
[10:02] Sara Nguyen: do you do key wrapping with asymmetric keys, e.g., we maintain an RSA or EC key and you encrypt DEKs with it?
[10:11] Jordan Lee: envelope encryption with asymmetric wrapping is supported; many customers use RSA/ECC CMKs in their KMS to wrap symmetric DEKs.
[10:20] Maya Rivera: is there support for customer-side encryption prior to sending to Redwood — we want end-to-end where we encrypt payloads and only Redwood processes ciphertext with a token.
[10:31] Priya Shah: client-side encryption is possible for some workloads but it limits Redwood's ability to do model-specific operations unless you provide decryption in your environment; for some use cases you can do partial homomorphic patterns or transform data before sending. It's more complex; we'd treat that as custom work.
[10:52] Daniel Cho: okay let's talk about audit artifacts — what exactly do you provide for SOC2/ISO audits?
[11:00] Alex Morgan: we provide system logs, access logs, key usage logs (where available), change management notes, and our SOC 2 report and ISO attestation. For BYOK we include KMS logs you retain plus correlated Redwood operational logs.
[11:15] Liam O'Connor: can you provide a sample of the log schema? timestamps, request id, node id, key id?
[11:22] Priya Shah: yes — we will share sample log lines and a schema doc. We include request id, model id, node id, encrypted payload hash, and key id references (no plaintext).
[11:34] Maya Rivera: what about RBAC/SSO — can we restrict who in our team can trigger key rotations or view key metadata in Redwood console?
[11:44] Alex Morgan: yes RBAC is pluggable — we integrate with SSO providers (SAML/OIDC) and you can map roles to permissions. For Private we recommend SAML-based SSO with SCIM provisioning to tie into your IAM.
[11:58] Sarah (sic) Nguyen: small note — we use Okta, SCIM is important for us.
[12:04] Alex Morgan: Okta is supported. We'll include an SSO/SCIM guide.
[12:09] Daniel Cho: any encryption certifications or third-party validation for your runtime?
[12:16] Priya Shah: our platform is SOC 2 Type II and we have ISO attestations; some runtime subsystems undergo pen tests. For HSM integrations we rely on vendor FIPS attestations.
[12:31] Liam O'Connor: curious about key usage telemetry — do you ever log token payload hashes that could be reversible?
[12:39] Jordan Lee: we log cryptographic hashes for correlation (salted hashes) and avoid storing reversible payloads. We'll work with you on redaction rules.
[12:49] Maya Rivera: ok next — regulatory traceability: if an auditor asks for proof we rotated keys on X date, can you provide chain of custody?
[12:58] Alex Morgan: yes we can provide an audit trail: KMS logs + Redwood correlated events + node restart markers. We'll package it as an auditor-friendly bundle.
[13:10] Daniel Cho: on the mention of node restarts — how do you coordinate rollouts to avoid large cache churn?
[13:18] Priya Shah: rollout strategies include staged evictions, canary nodes, and warm-up scripts. We can also pre-warm caches with unwraps before traffic cutover.
[13:30] Sara Nguyen: question about backups — are encrypted backups made and where are the keys?
[13:36] Jordan Lee: backups are encrypted at rest; keys for backups are managed by your KMS in BYOK scenarios or Redwood-managed KMS otherwise. For extra assurance you can require separate CMKs for backups.
[13:50] Daniel Cho: do you support key versioning and rollback?
[13:55] Priya Shah: yes KMS versioning is supported and Redwood can reference specific key versions in config. Rollback is managed at the orchestration level.
[14:05] Maya Rivera: i want to understand the minimal trust boundary if we let Redwood manage keys — what's the residual risk?
[14:12] Alex Morgan: if Redwood manages keys, we hold CMKs in our KMS and manage rotation; your data is still encrypted but you rely on our controls and attestations. BYOK reduces trust by keeping CMKs in your control. We'll provide a comparison doc.
[14:30] Liam O'Connor: any known incidents in the last 24 months related to key leakage?
[14:35] Priya Shah: none to disclose; we perform regular pen tests and rotate creds. We'll share the relevant summary in the SOC2 material.
[14:45] Daniel Cho: great. let's cover a scenario: we want to keep PII out of logs and have keys in our KMS (AWS). We also want 24/7 low-latency inference in us-east-1. What's the recommended architecture?
[14:58] Jordan Lee: recommended: Redwood Private running in your VPC in us-east-1, KMS CMKs in the same region, HSM proxy if you use on-prem HSM, short cache TTLs if you require rapid revoke, and SIEM integration for audit logs. Use SAML Okta for RBAC, and disable token telemetry for payloads.
[15:20] Sara Nguyen: what's the ops overhead for Private compared to Dedicated? we want minimal ops but max control.
[15:27] Alex Morgan: Private is more hands-on; we provide a managed ops assistance add-on. Dedicated is a middle ground with reserved capacity but Redwood-managed infra. We'll include a cost/ops comparison doc.
[15:41] Daniel Cho: fine. any blocker for us to run a POC with BYOK?
[15:45] Priya Shah: no blockers technically; we'll need network access for anything talking to your KMS/HSM, an scp for config, and a signed agreement.
[15:55] Alex Morgan: ok let's list out immediate deliverables — i'll send the KMS integration guide, priya will send latency notes and examples, and we'll schedule a scoping call.
[16:05] Daniel Cho: sounds good. final question: are there restrictions on key algorithms or sizes we must follow?
[16:12] Jordan Lee: we recommend AES-256 for DEKs and RSA/ECDSA for wrapping as per vendor guidance. We support common algorithms supported by KMS vendors.
[16:24] Maya Rivera: thanks. anything else on compliance — are there specific clauses we should expect in contracts for BYOK?
[16:30] Alex Morgan: yes BYOK typically has terms around key custody and audit access; legal will follow up.
[16:35] Liam O'Connor: can you provide a short integration checklist?
[16:39] Priya Shah: yes will include network, IAM roles, sample unwrap, and tests.
[16:45] Daniel Cho: thanks all.
[16:48] Alex Morgan: recap and next steps: deliver docs, schedule scoping, provide SOC2/ISO. Everybody ok with that?
[16:55] Maya Rivera: yes we'll look for the docs and reply with internal stakeholders for the scoping call.
[17:02] Sara Nguyen: ok i'll coordinate firewall and HSM contacts.
[17:06] Alex Morgan: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with links.
[17:10] Daniel Cho: thanks. bye.

End transcript.
